statement: The second part of the lecture designs a super fast key-value store on very commodity hardware (cheap magnetic hard disks) that supports read, write, update and delete with full persistence.
detail: The teacher wants the best of everything: read, write, update, delete, persistence.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: building a super fast key-value store on top of very commodity hardware, cheap magnetic hard disk.

statement: In the storage hierarchy (CPU/L1 cache, memory, SSD, magnetic disk, tape), SSDs sit closer to memory than magnetic hard disks in both speed and cost.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: SSDs are more closer to memory as compared to hard disk with respect to speed and with respect to cost.

statement: SSDs are fast but very costly compared to magnetic disks, so huge amounts of data are stored on magnetic disk storage, not on SSDs.
detail: We are all used to SSDs, but getting an SSD is very costly compared with magnetic disk storage.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So which is where you are storing huge amount of data. You don't store it on SSDs.

statement: A magnetic disk is the classic disk-based storage in which a head moves across while the disk spins underneath it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's that classic disk based storage where you have a head, head rotates like this in this motion while your disk spins.

statement: A read of a byte offset in a file is translated into a physical location: a particular disk, a particular sector on it, and an offset within that sector.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it then translates into on this disk, in this sector, at this offset it lies in.

statement: To serve a read, the disk rotates and the magnetic head physically moves to the location, reads that part and sends it to the device driver, from where it goes to user space; every new read at another place needs another movement.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: magnetic head comes to that point, read that particular part and sends it to the device driver, and then it goes to the user space

statement: The mechanical movement on a magnetic disk (moving the head, rotating the disk) is the most time-consuming part of disk I/O.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Mechanical movement that happens on the disk is the most time-consuming process.

statement: The key-value store must support only put, get and delete, but must not miss out on persistence: every put is immediately flushed to disk.
detail: When a student reached for an in-memory structure, the teacher clarified: 'When I say put it, it is to immediately flush to the disk.'
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we want to support operations like put, get, delete. That's it.

statement: A student proposed a memtable/SSTable-style structure (a sorted map held in memory) for the key-value store; the teacher rejected it because every put must be persisted to disk immediately.
detail: Teacher: 'No, no, immediately. I want to persist immediately.'
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: it looks like fitting in the way that structure of a memtable or SSTable works, you have something in memory as a sorted map.

statement: To persist every put immediately, keep a ledger-like file (a write-ahead style log) where every change is appended at the end instead of being placed where it belongs.
detail: A student proposed it; the teacher asked 'what is write-ahead?' and the student described a file to which every change is appended at the end; the teacher answered 'Perfect.' The student already worried about deletes in this design.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: the best thing is like you create a ledger, where you start adding each and every

statement: Appending suits a magnetic disk best: the head is already where the last write ended, so there is no seek time for the head and no waiting for the disk to spin to the right sector; you just add more blocks at that point.
detail: Student's reasoning ('That's the best I can do to get the benefit out of the characteristic of the disk'), answered by the teacher with 'Perfect.'
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: A seek time, neither you need that your cylinder has to spin and reach to the right sector.

statement: Put on the append-only file: for put K1 V1 the key and value are appended to the end of the file; later puts (K2 V2, K3 V3) are appended after it.
detail: The teacher builds the design one operation at a time: first make put as good as possible, then get, then delete.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I will just create new entries into this file. K2 V2 and then K3 V3.

statement: An update (put K1 V1' on an existing key) is also just appended: you do not go back to find the old K1 and change it; the old entry becomes obsolete. Any put is appended no matter what.
detail: Student proposal; the student added that some other process must mark obsolete data or deletions (a tombstone-like process). Teacher: 'No matter what. That's the best way. Perfect.'
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: But idea is always any put comes, you go and add no matter what.

statement: Appending every put to the file is how you get the maximum performance out of the put operation on a cheap magnetic disk.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So this is how you get the max performance out of put operation on a cheap magnetic disk storage.

statement: A student suggested also remembering, in a memory table, the address where each key's entry starts on disk; the teacher deferred this until get is discussed.
detail: Teacher: 'We'll come to that. Let's first get the max performance out of it.' The idea returns as the in-memory hash table of key to offset (K3-022).
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: I need to have K1 and wherever the K1 is started, that sector address in somewhere in my memory table or somewhere else.

statement: A student proposed deleting a key by going back to its entry and overwriting its value with a special value that never occurs (e.g. -1 if values are always positive); this is not allowed in an append-only file, which cannot be written at earlier locations.
detail: Teacher: 'But this is append only file. You cannot write to any other location.'
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: we can go to this key and set the value to be something which will never occur.

statement: An append-only file can be read anywhere in its earlier content, but nothing can be written to an earlier location; writes only go to the end.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you can only read from the previous stuff, but you cannot write to a previous stuff. That's what append only file does.

statement: Delete in an append-only file is a put with a special value: append an entry such as K2 with a marker value saying the key is deleted.
detail: Reasoned from first principles: the only thing allowed is to append, so append something that tells K2 is deleted. The student proposed appending 'K2 with minus one'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So effectively your delete operation is equal to put operation with some special value.

statement: Because put is O(1), the bare minimum, a delete implemented as a put is also super efficient; put and delete are both solved.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Because put was order one like bare minimum, delete also becomes super efficient.

statement: A student proposed the naive get: scan all entries of the file (which holds several entries for the same key) and return the latest one.
detail: Teacher's correction: that seems very poor, because get must also have the best performance ('Return the latest one that seems very poor').
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Just start looking at all the entries and return the latest one.

statement: A student again reached for an SSTable-like structure to speed up get; the teacher redirected to a simple hash table, stressing that an SSTable and a hash table are very different things.
detail: Teacher: 'Simple hash table, right? SSTable is very different, hash table is very different, right?'
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: my mind like overall is still going towards what Hemant had mentioned earlier, like around having an SSTable sort of structure here.

statement: Get is made fast with an in-memory hash table mapping each key to the offset of its latest entry in the append-only file (the offset, not the value); it is updated as soon as an entry is appended, and a read goes straight to that offset.
detail: Student proposal accepted by the teacher.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: we update the hash table as well, so the offset of it, correct, not the actual value.

statement: An append-only file allows random reads but not random writes, which is why reading at a stored offset is fine.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: in append only file you're allowed to do random reads, but you're not allowed to do random writes.

statement: Put with the index: first write the entry to disk and note its offset, then update the in-memory hash table (put K1 V1 -> K1 points at O1; K2 -> O2; K3 -> O3). On put K1 V1', append it first, then repoint K1 in the hash table to the new offset (O4).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I first write it to the disk over here and note with the offset, and then I update my in-memory hash table

statement: Delete with the index: remove the key's entry from the in-memory hash table; if a key has no entry in the hash table, it does not exist.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I just remove the entry from my memory hash table. If the entry does not exist, it does not exist.

statement: Get flow: look the key up in the in-memory hash table; if there is no entry return 404 (not found); if there is, go to that offset in the file and read the value.
detail: Student's answer, confirmed by the teacher ('Perfect').
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: You look it up in the in-memory hash table. If the entry is not there, you simply return 404 or something.

statement: If the machine dies, the in-memory hash table is lost; on restart, go through the entire file and rebuild the index.
detail: A student noted the rebuild can take a long time; the teacher said that is fine.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When you restart, you just go through this entire file and rebuild this index.

statement: With this design get, put and delete are each O(1), doing the bare minimum: the maximum one can get on a cheap magnetic disk, with full persistence for read, write, update and delete.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So it's the max that we could get out of this on a cheap magnetic disk storage.

statement: Rebuilding the index on restart lowers availability because coming back takes a lot of time; the teacher accepts this for the naive design and says there are ways to make it better.
detail: Raised by a student when asked what could go wrong.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: availability is less because when you come back again, it takes a lot of time.

statement: The design assumes all index entries fit in memory: you are limited by how much index (the keys, not the values) fits in RAM, so you can store only as many keys as you can keep in memory.
detail: Raised by a student; the teacher confirmed it as a limitation.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So you can add only as many keys as many you can keep in memory.

statement: Because the design only appends and never collects disk garbage, the single file grows huge and the system eventually runs out of disk space.
detail: Student's point; teacher: 'Correct. So file grows out to be huge.'
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: eventually our system will go out of space because we are not collecting anything from the disk.

statement: A student proposed using multiple files on disk instead of one, and scrubbing a file no longer being appended to: read it and write a new file containing only the keys still required, dropping deleted keys.
detail: The teacher accepted the multiple-files idea and deferred the scrubbing to a separate process (merge and compaction).
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: idea is don't just have one file on the disk. So we'll have to create multiple files

statement: With multiple files, at any point in time writes go to only one file; the other files become immutable.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So at any point in time, write will only go to one file. Yes. Other file becomes immutable.

statement: A student argued the disk needs room for three files at most (one being written, one being read, one being created); the teacher corrected that reads are not tied to one file: a read goes to whichever file holds the key, including the file being written.
detail: The student kept arguing about reading a file to rebuild it without its deleted offsets; the teacher said that belongs to a different process discussed later and first asked for the criterion to switch files.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: At max at any given time I think we would need a space of three files, one that we are writing to, one that...
flags: check: speaker of "How will you do it?" at 02:16:57 (Teacher?)

statement: A student proposed choosing when to switch to a new file by dividing the disk space by two or three.
detail: Teacher's correction: he illustrated it (a 100 TB disk would get 10 TB files, 10 files) and said there are more problems with that, leading to the file-system limit and small-file threshold (K3-037, K3-038).
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: In disk space, it will be either divided by two or three based on the approach that we have.
flags: check: speaker of "Now there are more problems to this" at 02:18:22 (Teacher?)

statement: Problems with very large files: scanning a single file cannot build the in-memory index concurrently (a motivation for more, smaller partitions), and garbage collection on smaller partitions can be more consistent.
detail: Student's answer; the teacher then added an even bigger reason (K3-037).
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: if you're just scanning a single file, you can't concurrently build indexes in memory. So that's one problem.
flags: check: teacher's verdict implicit ("The biggest one of all")

statement: The biggest reason not to use huge files is the file system limitation: a file system may not support files larger than one terabyte; BTRFS and NTFS each have their limits.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: file system limitation. It is very much possible that your file system does not support more than one terabyte file.

statement: Rather than waiting for one huge file to fill, keep smaller files (e.g. 100 MB or 1 GB) and start writing a new file as soon as the size threshold is crossed.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: keep smaller files. Let's say 100 MB files or let's say 1 GB files. As soon as that threshold checks off, you move forward

statement: Files are numbered in sequence (file 001, 002, 003, 004 ...); at any time exactly one file is active and receives all writes, and every other file is read-only but can still be read.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So at any given point in time one file will be active where all the writes are going. Everything else becomes read only.

statement: File rotation: every time the active file crosses its size limit, a new file is created and writes continue in it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So this is typically called as file rotation.

statement: With multiple files, the in-memory index stores for each key which file it is in and at which offset; a get finds the key, goes to that file and offset, reads the content and sends it back.
detail: Previously the index stored only the offset.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Want to store that this key is present in this file. In this offset.

statement: The rotated files contain many stale entries (keys overwritten later, e.g. the old K1) and deleted entries (e.g. K2), which waste disk space.
topic: storage engines > bitcask > merge and compaction
speaker: teacher
verbatim: there are a lot of stale entries, a lot of deleted entries.

statement: Merge and compaction: while the active file keeps taking writes, a process iterates through the read-only files and writes one new file combining them without the stale and deleted entries; once the new file is written the old files are deleted forever.
detail: Example: three read-only files are merged into a fourth file.
topic: storage engines > bitcask > merge and compaction
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Using these three files you create a fourth file which is a combination of these three in which you are not copying the stale entries

statement: After merge and compaction the offsets change, so the in-memory index must be updated for every entry that moved into the new file.
topic: storage engines > bitcask > merge and compaction
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you also have to update this in-memory index for the entries that are just moved to this new file.

statement: Implementing merge and compaction: iterate through the files keeping track of the keys seen, replace older values with newer ones, and periodically flush to disk.
detail: The teacher calls this the classic way to do merge and compaction.
topic: storage engines > bitcask > merge and compaction
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Just iterate through this file, keep keeping track of data that you are having.

statement: Disk utilization follows a sawtooth pattern: it grows as writes come in and drops suddenly every time merge and compaction runs, then grows again.
topic: storage engines > bitcask > merge and compaction > sawtooth
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You'll see this sawtooth pattern in your disk consumption.

statement: The sawtooth must stay below the disk's maximum capacity (a 1 TB disk cannot let it grow beyond 1 TB); its shape is used to configure the merge and compaction frequency and determines the database's performance.
topic: storage engines > bitcask > merge and compaction > sawtooth
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So if your disk is let's say one terabyte big, you cannot let this grow beyond one terabyte, right?

statement: Merging too frequently means too much garbage collection, taking CPU away from actual work; merging too rarely lets a lot of work accumulate. The frequency should be smooth enough not to drop performance.
topic: storage engines > bitcask > merge and compaction > sawtooth
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If you, let's say, dump too frequently, it would have too much of garbage collection happening

statement: The design has only two configurable parameters: the merge and compaction frequency, and the file rotation threshold (how big a file may grow).
detail: The teacher first said 'disk rotation threshold' and corrected himself to 'file rotation threshold'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You only have two configurable parameters over here. First is merge and compaction frequency. And second is disk rotation threshold.

statement: Set the two parameters by monitoring the sawtooth pattern while building the store, and when you design such a database, expose them as configurable parameters to whoever you ship it to.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: when you are designing this database, you provide this as a configurable parameters to your folks, right?

statement: This append-only design with merge and compaction is a pretty standard approach and the best one can do on a cheap magnetic disk: best read, write, update and delete with efficient disk usage, almost as fast as SSDs.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is a pretty standard approach and this is the best we can do on disk, on a cheap magnetic disk storage, right?

statement: On SSDs the design still helps but not as significantly, because SSDs do not use a rotating disk; they use flash memory, which already handles this very optimally.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: On SSD you will still get benefits but not as significant because SSDs don't go with disk based approach

statement: Writing 'key value' to the file is too casual: files are read by blocks, not line by line, so a disk-based store needs a defined record format for each entry.
detail: Even the word dictionary problem was simplified to 'word comma meaning' read line by line.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Files are read by blocks. So how do you actually define a format, a record format?

statement: Every database (MySQL, Postgres, MongoDB, Redis, ...) serializes data to disk in its own record format designed to make reads efficient.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: pick any database, whenever they're serializing things to disk, they have their own format in which they write it

statement: Reading a record until a newline is a bad approach: reading one byte at a time until '\n' means one disk I/O per byte, which makes things very slow; the teacher calls it code a school kid would write.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: let's say you read one byte at a time until you hit a slash n. How many disk IOs are you making?

statement: At any offset you should know exactly how many bytes to read to get the complete key-value entry, so the whole entry is read in one shot.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you have to read the exact number of bytes you are supposed to, so that you get that entire data in one shot.

statement: Record format: before the key and value, write the key size and the value size (each a 4-byte integer, 8 bytes together), telling how many bytes the key and the value take.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you'll write key size and value size as well. So first you write key size, which tells you how many bytes is key.

statement: Reading a record takes two disk I/Os: first read the 8-byte header and interpret the first 4 bytes as key size and the next 4 as value size; then add them up and read that many bytes in one more I/O, splitting them into key and value.
detail: This gives read predictability; the header is like the metadata header of the earlier word-dictionary problem.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You read this eight bytes, interpret first four bytes as this, second four bytes as value size, then you sum it up

statement: The word dictionary should also be stored this way (word size, meaning size, then word and meaning); it was written as CSV earlier only because that is easy, and its design can now be updated with this record format.
case_study: Word dictionary problem from the first half of the lecture.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is similar what you will do in even in word dictionary also. Word size, meaning size.

statement: A database must be fault tolerant: if the machine crashes while a gigantic value is being written, the write fails and the entry is corrupt; the data cannot be fixed, but the store must at least know the entry lost its integrity and not serve it.
detail: Many people stop at key size / value size; the teacher says they should not.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: What if you are writing a gigantic value and while writing the value, the machine crashed?

statement: A partially written entry is dangerous: if another entry is written after it, reading 'value size' bytes from the broken entry would run into the next entry.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If you read value size number of bytes over here, it would penetrate into other entry that you have.

statement: The only way to detect corruption is a CRC (cyclic redundancy check) / checksum: a hash over key size, value size, key and value, computed on the record built in memory and stored with it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Simple hash of all the values, key size, value size, key value, everything.

statement: The CRC goes on the leftmost side of the record and is the first thing written and flushed, because it is the bare minimum needed to know something is corrupted; it cannot be written at the end.
detail: Compared with distributed ID generators, which put the timestamp on the leftmost side.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You cannot write CRC in the end. You write CRC in the beginning.

statement: Good persistent record formats put the CRC on the leftmost side, e.g. the Postgres commit log file and the MySQL binlog.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Postgres commit log file, CRC on the leftmost side. MySQL bin log, CRC on the leftmost side.

statement: Network formats also put the CRC first, because those are the first bytes received and tell whether the incoming data is corrupted.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Pick any network format, you'd always say CRC at the first, because that's the first byte or the first set of bytes that you...

statement: Final record format: CRC, timestamp (just for conflicts), key size, value size, key, value.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: CRC, time stamp just for conflicts, key size, value size, key and value.

statement: Write the header part first, then the key in one disk write and the (possibly gigantic) value in another. If the first write fails, the entry does not exist; if a later write fails, the CRC will not match on read, and the user is told the entry is corrupted, so corrupted data is never served.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You are not serving corrupted data to your users ever.

statement: Recovery from a corrupted entry is mostly heuristics: ignore the entry (for example during merge and compaction) and assume the write never came, since corrupted data cannot be recovered anyway.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You ignore that entry in merge and compaction and whatnot. You assume that the write never came your way

statement: When designing storage, question whether CSV and reading until newline is the best way; use a record format with key size, value size, key, value and CRC integrity checks for durability and fault tolerance.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Key size, value size, key value, all of this with CRCs, integrity checks, durability, fault tolerance.

statement: With file rotation, each in-memory index entry holds, for a key, the file it is in, the record size, the offset, and a timestamp for conflicts and meta information; entries can point to any file while writes go only to the active file.
detail: Recap of get and file rotation from the prepared notes: all operations are key-value records in this format appended one after another; the file grows too big, hence rotation.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now we need to store that this key is present in this file, the entire record size is this, add this offset

statement: Merging Bitcask files is not like the merge step of merge sort, because the entries are not sorted; instead load entries into a temporary hash table, replacing a key when a later entry appears, and periodically flush it to disk without the stale or deleted entries.
detail: The teacher says it is not difficult and encourages writing the code.
topic: storage engines > bitcask > merge and compaction
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's not similar to merge of merge sort, because here the order can be anything. It's not sorted.

statement: The sawtooth pattern determines the maximum file size and the merge frequency needed to keep disk usage under the cap; if usage crosses the disk's capacity, the system crashes. Very frequent merges are not good and very infrequent ones breach the cap, so keep it at the optimum.
topic: storage engines > bitcask > merge and compaction > sawtooth
speaker: teacher
verbatim: As soon as it crosses the cap of it, your system would crash, right?

statement: The main limitation of the design: all keys must fit in memory. Values are on disk, but the in-memory index holds keys and their offsets, so the number of keys that fit in memory bounds how many keys the database can store.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The limitation of the system is all the keys must fit in memory

statement: The strength of the design is O(1) reads and writes, where O(1) means the bare minimum the disk has to do when asked to write.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When I say order one, it's a bare minimum that your disk has to do when it is there to write

statement: The design gives very high write throughput and very low write latency, because it does the bare minimum disk I/O.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You get very high write throughput. You get very low latency, write very low latency.

statement: A read costs one memory lookup and one random disk read, after which the data is sent back.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Reads, one memory lookup, one random read, get a data, send it back

statement: The design reaches I/O saturation of the physical device (and of the network), which is good: nothing waits idle for I/O, so you get the most out of the underlying hardware.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You actually get IO saturation. Your physical device IO will be saturated, and that's a good thing

statement: Backups are easy because the data is normal files: copy and paste the files and you have a backup.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: backups are easy. Control C, control V, these files and you have backup.

statement: The database just designed is Bitcask, an embedded database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The database that we just designed is called Bitcask. It's an embedded database.

statement: An embedded database is a library rather than a central server everyone connects to (unlike a MySQL server); SQLite is an example, and Bitcask has no separate server.
detail: The teacher had earlier shared a video on what embedded databases are.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Bitcask is not like a MySQL server that was spinning up and everyone connects to that.

statement: Uber uses Bitcask in production for its main ride-hailing service.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So Bitcask is used by Uber in production for their main ride-hailing service.

statement: Since Bitcask is embedded, Uber uses Riak as its main database; Riak is a simple key-value store that uses Bitcask as its back-end.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Uber uses Riak as their main database. Riak is a simple key-value store and Riak uses Bitcask as a back-end.

statement: Riak is to Bitcask what Elasticsearch is to Lucene: Elasticsearch is an HTTP wrapper over Lucene, and Riak is a wrapper over Bitcask.
detail: Repeated at 02:39:26-02:40:36: 'just like what Elasticsearch did to Lucene, Riak does it with Bitcask.'
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So like how Elasticsearch is an HTTP wrapper over Lucene, similarly, Riak is a wrapper over Bitcask.

statement: Riak's responsibility is to make Bitcask distributed: master-slave architecture, consensus, a proxy that routes requests, consistent hashing and data movement, with each Bitcask holding a mutually exclusive set of data; Bitcask underneath gets the most out of the disk when storing and retrieving.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So Riak's responsibility is to make Bitcask distributed.

statement: The append-only file is the magic behind Bitcask getting the most out of cheap commodity hardware.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the append-only file that we see is the magic behind getting the max out of cheap commodity hardware.

statement: Whenever a system claims high throughput with persistence, it is using an append-only file or something similar; if it is not, the teacher does not believe the high-throughput claim.
topic: storage engines > append-only file > high throughput
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So whenever you see anything that says we are high throughput, it means they are using append-only file.

statement: Bitcask is a really simple yet fabulous database that covers the intricate details: data integrity checks, record format, merge and compaction, and getting the most out of cheap commodity hardware; it is heavily used in production, as Riak's backend.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Data integrity checks, record format, merge and compaction, getting the max out of cheap commodity hardware.

statement: There is a paper on Bitcask, a Google search away, that learners can refer to.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: There is a paper on Bitcask which you can refer, just a Google search away.

statement: The teacher highly recommends implementing Bitcask yourself: it is not difficult, and building it gives a much deeper understanding of file I/O and of getting maximum performance.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I would highly recommend you to implement Bitcask.

statement: The teacher implemented Bitcask about five years ago and personally benchmarked it against on-disk and in-memory key-value stores on disks and SSDs; that is why he is sure how it gets maximum performance and saturates I/O.
detail: He first said six years, then corrected to five.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I did a personal benchmark, Bitcask versus key-value store, Bitcask versus on-disk key-value store, in-memory key-value store

statement: To benchmark your own Bitcask, set up Prometheus on a machine to monitor it continuously while running it; spend about a week of your time building it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You just need the Prometheus on a machine continuously monitoring it, run your Bitcask

statement: Next week is about high-throughput systems, extending the storage week: S3, video encoding, YouTube views counting and one more database. This week got high throughput on the storage side; next week on the compute side.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Next week is all about high throughput systems.

statement: Next Saturday starts with a deep discussion of S3 and its nitty-gritty; everything studied so far comes in handy when designing S3.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: next week Saturday we'll first discuss huge discussion on S3.

statement: Bitcask vs SSTable/memtable (LSM trees): the big difference is that an SSTable design keeps values in memory, while Bitcask does not; SSTables are also sorted, for a reason covered next week.
detail: A student asked whether LSM trees, SSTable and memtable are the same process as Bitcask. The student added sorting as a second difference; the teacher said the sorting leverages something else, to be covered in depth next week.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: In SSTable in memory, we'll be touching about SSTable next week. But in SSTable, you also store values in memory.
flags: check: probably Hemant, called as "heaven" at 02:43:05

statement: Bitcask persists every write immediately to disk by default, prioritising persistence while still getting the most out of the disk; a memtable buffers writes and then writes them, so data can be lost if memory goes down.
detail: The student suggested the memtable would have to be saved locally on every write; the teacher said in Bitcask that comes by default.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: In memtable, you buffer and then you write.
flags: asr: [?Every write, every write | asr: "Every day, every day"]

statement: Bitcask was taught first on purpose as the foundation; next week covers SSTable, memtable, LSM trees and high-throughput systems such as counting.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Next week we'll be touching upon SSTable, memtable, that part, LSM trees, high throughput systems when you do counting and all.

statement: The teacher came across Bitcask in a storage paper-reading course in college and was struck by how simple and beautiful it is; he recommends reading the paper, calling it fabulous.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I had this in my college paper reading. I took a course on storage readings and it was part of a paper reading thing.

statement: To create an append-only file, open the file in append mode 'a' (besides r, w, r+, w+); you do not reserve space (e.g. 1 GB) upfront - the file system, through system calls, handles laying out the file and breaking it into pieces.
detail: A student asked whether to preallocate a contiguous 1 GB file and track how much was written, or just write incrementally with simple file APIs.
topic: storage engines > append-only file > file system
speaker: teacher
verbatim: There is an option called a. A is an append-only option.

statement: File systems (BTRFS, NTFS, ext2/3/4) do not allocate files back to back: when a file is created a large chunk is marked, and new files are placed in decent free space spaced out a bit, so a file growing slightly larger is not a problem.
topic: storage engines > append-only file > file system
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it's responsibility of the file system, BTRFS, NTFS, EXT234, whichever you are using, that when you are creating new files, it finds a...

statement: Deleted keys (entries with the special delete value) are handled in merge and compaction: when merging the immutable rotated files (e.g. two read-only files while a third is active), stale and deleted entries are skipped, so they are never copied to the new file.
detail: A student asked how the default delete value is handled in the merge.
topic: storage engines > bitcask > merge and compaction
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You skip the stale entries and the deleted entries. So that would never be copied on the disk.

statement: Merge implementation: buffer key-value pairs in an in-memory hash table, replacing a key when a newer entry appears (so the first K1 is skipped) and removing a key when a delete entry is found, then flush the hash table as the new file. This hash table is separate from the index.
topic: storage engines > bitcask > merge and compaction
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This hash table is different from the index that we spoke about. Index is separate.

statement: Implementing a small Bitcask surfaces the devils in the details, such as whether to merge files in the same or a different process and how to update the in-memory index; it takes about a week and is not really difficult.
detail: The teacher offers help by note if anyone gets stuck.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: How do you merge this two file in the same process, in different process? How will you update in-memory index that you have, right?

statement: The pattern assumes writing the whole value is not atomic but writing the checksum and header is; the teacher confirmed that writing the header is atomic.
detail: Student question on the CRC design.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: So like what we are saying here is writing the whole value is not atomic, but writing the checksum and the header is.

statement: Different file systems and kernels give different guarantees: the pattern assumes a header under the block size is written atomically by the kernel, but a kernel might not give that guarantee, so behaviour can differ across kernels.
detail: Student raised it; teacher: 'Now, your kernel might not give that guarantee.' The student noted a value can be 1 MB.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now, your kernel might not give that guarantee. Right.

statement: The header is tiny (fields of eight and four bytes, roughly 20 bytes), so in practice it will definitely be written.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this is eight bytes, four bytes, four bytes, four bytes, which means roughly four, four, five or 20, 20 bytes
flags: check: header byte arithmetic garbled ("four, four, five or 20")

statement: A student noted that more paranoid systems, where the kernel does not guarantee atomic header writes, use a separate WAL system, while this pattern is more performant.
detail: The teacher responded that this is exactly the interesting nitty-gritty (K3-108), without a direct verdict.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: generally there are also more paranoid systems where kernels don't guarantee this. So you do have a separate WAL system

statement: Integrity is almost never covered in system design overviews: people just say 'write it to a WAL file' without saying how; almost no one talks about security and integrity, but database internals deal with it.
detail: Only the occasional passionate engineer thinks about integrity; these details are what make you better every day.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: No one talks about integrity at all. No one talks about security and integrity.

statement: The teacher recommends Hussein Nasser's Medium blog posts on Postgres internals (record-level format, pages, source-code snippets), best read once you understand file I/O, e.g. after implementing Bitcask.

speaker: teacher
verbatim: He is posting Postgres internals like anything, like going into record level format and whatnot.

speaker: teacher
verbatim: The number of pages Postgres takes up to store meta information versus actual data. That just blew my mind.

statement: The 1 TB size of the word dictionary was chosen deliberately so that copying it to every API server becomes impossible on cost, to motivate network-attached storage and portability; it can be justified by assuming meanings include multimedia (audio, video).

statement: Asked how costly one S3 call per API request is, and whether caching or frequency-based storage is over-optimization: in the real world you have to do that; querying S3 directly was meant to show that pointed reads on S3 are possible.
case_study: Word dictionary problem from the first half of the lecture.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: my intention for that was I wanted to point out that it is possible to make pointed reads on S3.

statement: Pointed reads on S3 (e.g. of a particular order ID) enable a classic cold-storage / multi-tiered storage mechanism: move data from the hot tier to the cold tier to save cost while still keeping it seamlessly queryable on S3 (as with Athena), to be built next week.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this is a classic cold storage mechanism. They're moving data from hot tier to cold tier to save cost.

statement: For infrequent reads higher latency is acceptable, so data can be read from S3: S3 calls and network I/O are not cheap and S3 is not very performant, but S3 storage is very cheap.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And given it is infrequent, it's okay to have higher latency.

statement: Do not take MBs lightly: 170,000 words looks like a lot, yet multiplied by the per-entry index size the index turns out to be only MBs; M means a million bytes, which is not lightweight and still holds a huge amount of information.
detail: The word dictionary was used as an easy example to show how small indexes can be.
case_study: Word dictionary problem from the first half of the lecture.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we take MBs very lightly, but M stands for a million, a million bytes.

statement: Triggering a redeployment to reload the API servers uses rolling deployment, which cloud providers give out of the box: the load balancer stays, and servers are removed and added one at a time.

verbatim: By default, cloud provider gives you this out of the box. Rolling deployment is out of the box.

statement: Offsets in the index are byte positions where a record starts, not line numbers.

statement: The dictionary file's header holds the size of the index (the number of bytes of the index stored in the same file), not a location of a separate file: read the header, get the index size, read that many bytes to get the index, then start serving.
detail: The student had understood that only a location was stored.
case_study: Word dictionary problem from the first half of the lecture.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So you first read the header, you get the index size. Then you read these many bytes here, you get the index.

statement: On updates the header is recreated: the merge creates a whole new file with a new dictionary, a new index and a new header.
case_study: Word dictionary weekly updates from the first half of the lecture.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We are recreating this header.

statement: Sorting the dictionary was not introduced at first because there was no need; it came in when going into the details, because keeping it sorted makes merging the changelog into the original dictionary very easy and efficient.
case_study: Word dictionary weekly updates from the first half of the lecture.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We realized that keeping it sorted makes our merging very easy.

statement: A student worried that keeping a 170,000-record file sorted adds complexity (where to insert each new entry); the teacher answered that lookups use the index offset directly, and a new sorted dictionary is created by the merge, so nothing is inserted in place.
detail: The student then realised the new dictionary is built by merging; 'I thought that it should be sorted before.'
case_study: Word dictionary weekly updates from the first half of the lecture.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: keeping this file sorted will, would create another level of complexity. So how would we approach that?

statement: The original dictionary and the changelog are both sorted, so the merged new file is sorted and becomes the old file for next week's update; thanks to sortedness, merging is O(n) - one iteration over both files - instead of O(n^2).
case_study: Word dictionary weekly updates from the first half of the lecture.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Just one iteration over this file or both the files and you have this new file created. You don't have to do n square complexity.

statement: The whole domain of computer science is obsessed with sorted data because sortedness makes processes so simple.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: which is why the entire domain of computer science is obsessed with sorted data.
